speakers.stance: Post-postmodern philosopher (Closure); rejects both materialism and the soul as ways of locating the self. Expect the 'closure' framework.

speakers.name: Maria Balaska
speakers.stance: Philosopher (Wittgenstein and Lacan at the Limit) working on the edges of experience. Expect the limits-of-language angle.

questions: What does 'soul' explain that 'irreducible subject' does not?
If the self is neither in the brain nor a soul, what is a person that dies?
Is the decline of materialism a finding or a mood among philosophers?

reading.title: Closure: A Story of Everything
reading.note: Lawson's framework.

reading.title: Wittgenstein and Lacan at the Limit
reading.note: Balaska on meaning and the limits of experience.

terms.def: Everything, including mind, is ultimately physical.
Philosophy after the linguistic turn that abandons the idea that language mirrors reality — Lawson's self-description.

44.question: Has the West lost its way — and what would it have to change to avoid becoming a museum and a self-absorbed superpower?
44.why: Mahbubani has spent two decades telling Western audiences that Asia's rise is not a problem to be managed but a fact to be adapted to. This talk names five fallacies — the habits of thought that two centuries of dominance bred — and what replacing them would take.
case: The West mistook a 200-year anomaly of dominance for the natural order; the rest of the world was 'asleep' and has woken.
Its custodians — politicians, pundits, priests — kept preaching universal values while abandoning the pragmatism that built their success.
Fallacies include: that democracy exports, that the US can contain China, that Europe can stay relevant without strategy, that the rules-based order was ever neutral.
The fixes are humility, engagement with Asia on its own terms, and domestic renewal before foreign adventure.
objections: Mahbubani's account of China is consistently charitable; critics note it rarely mentions Xinjiang, Hong Kong or the Party's own fallacies.
Asia's rise is real but not uniform — Japan's stagnation, China's demography and debt, India's inequality complicate the story.
'The West' is not one actor; much of the diagnosis applies to Washington and not to Seoul, Warsaw or Helsinki.
Prophecies of Western decline have a century-long record of being early.

speakers.name: Kishore Mahbubani
speakers.stance: Former Singaporean ambassador to the UN and president of the Security Council; Has China Won?, The Asian 21st Century, Living the Asian Century. Expect a polished diplomat's provocation. He debates superpowers at 5:30pm in the International tent.

questions: Name a fallacy of China's custodians to match your five for the West.
Which Western country has adapted best to the Asian century, and what did it do?
Is the rules-based order worth saving, or only worth replacing?

reading.title: Has China Won?
reading.note: The argument at length.

reading.title: The Return of Great Power Rivalry
reading.note: The strongest case that democracies win these contests — the counter-view.

terms.def: The post-1945 system of institutions and norms, defended by the West and described by critics as Western rules.
The expectation that economic and political weight shifts decisively to Asia in the twenty-first century.

47.question: Pain now or pain later — which trade-offs are worth making for growth, and who decides?
47.why: Two people who made these calls inside the Treasury and the pensions system disagree across the aisle: cut or invest, spend or save. It is a debate in all but billing, and the rare kind where both sides have signed the cheques.
case: Hunt: fiscal credibility first — markets punish loose plans, and stability is the precondition for investment; growth comes from the supply side, tax on investment and planning.
Bell: under-investment is the British disease — public and private capital spending has lagged for decades, and austerity made it worse; borrow to invest and reform the state.
Both: pensions, housing and the tax base are where the real trade-offs live, and politics avoids them.
The honest position on either side names a loser.
objections: Hunt's stability case has to answer for the years of stagnation on his own watch; Bell's investment case for the interest bill on the borrowing.
'Invest' is doing a lot of work — investment in what, chosen by whom, with what record of delivery?
Neither side's framework has produced growth since 2008; maybe the trade-off is misframed.
Both are professional politicians now; the candour may be rationed.

speakers.name: Jeremy Hunt
speakers.stance: Conservative former Chancellor; the fiscal-credibility, supply-side case. See also his 12pm talk on optimism.

speakers.name: Torsten Bell
speakers.stance: Labour MP and Pensions Minister; formerly chief executive of the Resolution Foundation and author of Great Britain? Expect data-heavy argument for investment and for fixing living standards at the bottom.

questions: Name a cut you would make and a tax you would raise. No abstractions.
What is the evidence that the investment you propose would pay back — and on what timescale?
Which trade-off did you get wrong in office?

reading.title: Great Britain? How We Get Our Future Back
reading.note: Bell's diagnosis from the Resolution Foundation years.

reading.title: Can We Be Great Again?
reading.note: Hunt's post-Treasury view.

terms.def: Self-imposed limits on borrowing and debt that constrain what a Chancellor can do.
Real disposable income after housing — Bell's preferred measure of whether policy works.

53.question: Did Gandhi's philosophy of non-violence uphold the caste system rather than challenge it?
53.why: Gandhi is the West's model of moral politics. Dwivedi, working from a tradition of Indian dissent that runs through Ambedkar, argues his thought was an 'anti-politics' that preserved a hierarchy condemning millions to servitude. It is a demolition of an icon by someone who has read him closely.
case: Gandhi defended varnashrama — the caste order — as a natural division of labour, and opposed Ambedkar's demand for separate electorates for Dalits (the 1932 fast).
His non-violence was directed at the British state, not at the violence of caste; 'Harijan' uplift left the structure intact.
The Western myth of Gandhi is convenient: a saint of peace that lets the caste question disappear from the story of Indian freedom.
Ambedkar's alternative — annihilation of caste, constitutional rights — is the real philosophy of Indian liberation.
objections: Gandhi's views on caste changed over decades; late Gandhi attacked untouchability and, arguably, caste itself.
Non-violence as a strategy mobilised millions across caste lines; judging it by its silences ignores what it did.
Ambedkar and Gandhi were rivals, but reducing Gandhi to a caste apologist is also a myth, from the other side.
The critique of the 'Western myth' can flatten how Gandhi is contested within India today, including by the Hindu right.

speakers.name: Divya Dwivedi
speakers.stance: Philosopher at IIT Delhi; Gandhi and Philosophy and Indian Philosophy, Indian Revolution (with Shaj Mohan). Expect a fierce, theoretically dense reading. She debates philosophical systems at 7pm and freedom on Sunday morning.

questions: What did Gandhi say about caste in his last years — and does it change the verdict?
If non-violence was anti-politics, what was Ambedkar's politics, and did it succeed?
How is Gandhi used by the Indian right today, and does your critique help or hurt them?

reading.title: Annihilation of Caste
reading.note: The undelivered speech that is the foundation of the critique — with Gandhi's reply and Ambedkar's rejoinder.

reading.title: Gandhi and Philosophy: On Theological Anti-Politics
reading.note: The book behind the talk.

terms.def: The Hindu ordering of society into hereditary occupational groups that Gandhi long defended as natural.
The agreement extracted by Gandhi's fast that replaced separate Dalit electorates with reserved seats — the hinge of the Gandhi–Ambedkar rivalry.

54.question: Did the UN, the courts and the human rights bodies fail Gaza — and if so, what were they for?
54.why: Finkelstein, son of Holocaust survivors and the most contested scholar of Israel–Palestine, argues the institutions built to prevent atrocity did not. Roger Hearing, a BBC journalist, holds him to the arguments his work has provoked. Expect the most charged room of the weekend.
case: International law was clear — on proportionality, on collective punishment, on the ICJ's provisional measures — and was not enforced.
The institutions failed not from ignorance but from the vetoes and dependencies built into them; 'failure' was structural.
The human rights bodies documented and then were ignored; documentation without enforcement is theatre.
The lesson is either to rebuild enforcement or to stop pretending the system protects anyone.
objections: Finkelstein's critics argue his framing of the conflict omits Hamas's own violations and the hostages; an account of institutional failure has to cover both sides' crimes.
Institutions 'fail' whenever great powers disagree — that is a description of the UN since 1945, not a special case.
The ICJ and ICC did act (provisional measures, arrest warrants); the failure was of states, not courts.
The rhetorical intensity of Finkelstein's work has cost him academic standing; listeners should separate the claims from the tone.

speakers.name: Norman Finkelstein
speakers.stance: Political scientist; The Holocaust Industry, Gaza: An Inquest into Its Martyrdom, Gaza's Gravediggers. Expect forensic use of the record, moral absolutism about law, and no softening. He also debates morality at noon.

speakers.name: Roger Hearing
speakers.stance: Interviews. Former BBC World Service journalist; expect challenge on the counter-arguments.

questions: Which institution did what it was built to do in Gaza, if any?
What enforcement mechanism would you design that great powers could not veto?
How should the same standards apply to Hamas, and where does your account of institutional failure address that?

reading.title: Gaza: An Inquest into Its Martyrdom
reading.note: His documentary method applied to earlier Gaza wars.

reading.title: ICJ, South Africa v. Israel — Order of 26 January 2024
reading.note: The provisional measures at the centre of the institutional argument; read the order itself.

terms.def: Interim orders by the ICJ while a case is pending — binding, but with no enforcement beyond the Security Council.
In the law of war, the rule that expected civilian harm must not be excessive relative to the concrete military advantage.

57.question: Is punishment a moral necessity — or does the urge to punish have darker roots that prisons only feed?
57.why: West teaches philosophy in prisons and grew up in a family in and out of them. His question is not whether crime should have consequences but what we are doing when we want someone to suffer — and whether the wanting says more about us than about them.
case: The satisfaction of seeing someone punished is a feeling, and feelings have histories: envy, fear, the need to feel clean by contrast.
Prisons rarely rehabilitate; they reliably degrade — so the urge is not being served by its stated justification.
People who have done terrible things are, in the classroom, recognisably people; the philosophical discussion changes both parties.
Asking 'am I as good as I think?' is the beginning of a less punitive society.
objections: Retribution is not sadism: giving wrongdoers what they deserve is a moral idea with a long pedigree (Kant thought it obligatory).
Victims exist; a philosophy of punishment that centres the punisher's psychology can forget them.
Deterrence and incapacitation are justifications that survive even if the urge is ugly.
Prison-philosophy classes are moving but small; the policy question is about the other 80,000.

speakers.name: Andy West
speakers.stance: Philosopher and prison educator, author of The Life Inside (2022), the memoir that inspired the BBC drama Waiting for the Out. Expect stories from the classroom and a case built on them.

questions: What should happen to someone who has killed, on your view — concretely, on the day after the verdict?
Is there a form of punishment you would defend, and what makes it different?
What did a prisoner teach you that changed the argument?

reading.title: The Life Inside
reading.note: The book; philosophy, prison and family in one.

reading.title: Discipline and Punish
reading.note: The classic on what punishment does besides punishing.

terms.def: Punishment is justified because it is deserved, independent of consequences.
Punishment justified by its power to change the offender — the aim prisons claim and mostly miss.

60.question: Is economics a science — or a discipline whose models of self-correcting equilibrium missed 2008 and will miss the next crash?
60.why: Keen predicted the 2008 crisis from private-debt dynamics that mainstream models ignore by construction. His claim is not that economists got a forecast wrong but that the discipline's foundations — equilibrium, rational agents, money as a veil — are false, and a new crash is built in.
case: Neoclassical models treat money and banks as neutral; in reality banks create money when they lend, and private debt drives booms and busts.
Economies are non-equilibrium systems: instability is endemic (Minsky), not an external shock to a stable machine.
The 2008 crash was foreseeable from debt-to-GDP dynamics; those who saw it were outside the mainstream.
The discipline defends its core by assumption, which is why it cannot learn.
objections: Mainstream macro has changed since 2008 — financial frictions, heterogeneous agents — more than Keen's critique allows.
Predicting crises from debt levels also produces false alarms; critics ask when Keen's 'next crash' has ever been dated.
'Not a science' proves too much: no social science predicts like physics, and economics still explains much.
Heterodox schools disagree with each other as much as with the mainstream; 'the emperor has no clothes' is not a tailor.

speakers.name: Steve Keen
speakers.stance: Post-Keynesian economist; Debunking Economics, The New Economics: A Manifesto; builder of the Minsky modelling software. Expect combative, model-driven argument. He debates free trade at 10:30am.

questions: What is the private-debt threshold at which you'd expect the next crisis, and where is the UK now?
Which mainstream economist has taken your critique seriously, and what changed?
If economics isn't a science, what should a Chancellor read instead?

reading.title: Debunking Economics
reading.note: The critique in full.

reading.title: Stabilizing an Unstable Economy
reading.note: The instability thesis Keen builds on.

terms.def: Banks create deposits when they lend; money is not a fixed stock allocated by savers.
The point in a credit boom when debt can no longer be serviced and asset prices collapse.

64.question: Did Heidegger find in poetry a truth philosophy cannot reach — and what could Anglophone poets teach that Hölderlin and Rilke could not?
64.why: Late Heidegger turned from philosophy to poetry as the site where being 'speaks'. Babich, a Nietzsche scholar and continental philosopher, takes the turn seriously and then pushes past it: what would it mean to think, and live, poetically now — with poets Heidegger never read?
case: For Heidegger, calculative thinking cannot grasp what poetic 'saying' can; Hölderlin and Rilke are not decoration but method.
Language is not a tool we use but the house we live in; poetry keeps that house open.
Anglophone poets — think of Dickinson, Hopkins, or Eliot — offer resources Heidegger's German canon lacked, including irony and doubt.
Thinking poetically is a way of living, not a style: attention, patience, letting things be.
objections: Heidegger's turn to poetry coincided with his Nazism and his silence about it; critics ask whether 'poetic thinking' was a retreat from responsibility.
Analytic philosophers reply that the claim 'poetry reaches truth philosophy cannot' needs an argument, not a mood.
Choosing which poets 'say being' is selection dressed as revelation.
Rilke and Hölderlin are hard even in German; an hour in a tent may give the flavour, not the thought.

speakers.name: Babette Babich
speakers.stance: Fordham philosopher, Nietzsche scholar (The Hallelujah Effect; Nietzsche's Philosophy of Science). Expect an erudite, digressive, quotable hour; she is sceptical of analytic philosophy's blind spots. She also debates beauty on Sunday.

questions: Which Anglophone poet would you set beside Hölderlin, and what does the poem know?
Does poetic thinking have anything to say to a physicist, or is it a different activity?
How should Heidegger's politics bear on his philosophy of poetry?

reading.title: '…Poetically Man Dwells…'
reading.by: Martin Heidegger (1951), in Poetry, Language, Thought
reading.note: The lecture on Hölderlin — twenty pages.

reading.title: Duino Elegies
reading.note: Read the first elegy in any translation before the talk.

terms.def: Heidegger's term for inhabiting the world attentively — what poetry, he claims, makes possible.
Heidegger's distinction between problem-solving reason and the thinking that lets things show themselves.

70.question: Have Western states expanded far beyond their proper bounds — and what would rolling them back look like?
70.why: From low-emission zones to policing to housing policy, Cunningham argues the state encroaches on freedom in the name of safety and sustainability. It is the libertarian case from inside a party that also wants a tougher state on borders and crime; the tension is part of the interest.
case: The modern state regulates where you drive, what you build, how you heat your home and what you may say; each rule is defensible and the sum is suffocating.
Safety and sustainability are used as trump cards that end debate; liberty needs a place at the table.
Local examples — ULEZ, planning, council enforcement — show how the reach grows without anyone voting for the whole.
Rolling back means sunset clauses, fewer agencies, and a burden of proof on the state.
objections: Reform UK's programme includes more police, more prisons and tighter borders — a bigger state, not a smaller one; which is it?
Clean-air zones and planning rules exist because of harms to others; liberty for the driver is cost for the asthmatic child.
'The state is too big' rarely names the pensions and NHS that are most of it.
A former prosecutor arguing against the state's reach will be asked which prosecutions she regrets.

speakers.name: Laila Cunningham
speakers.stance: Westminster City Councillor, former Crown Prosecution Service lawyer, Reform UK's 2028 London mayoral candidate. Expect a campaigning, example-driven case against state overreach. She also debates cultural Christianity at 1:30pm.

questions: Name three state functions you would abolish, and who would bear the cost.
Is a bigger police force compatible with a smaller state?
Which freedom has London lost in the last decade that its residents actually miss?

reading.title: 'Two Concepts of Liberty'
reading.note: Negative liberty — freedom from interference — is the concept in play.

reading.title: The Road to Serfdom
reading.note: The classic warning about the state's growth, cited by every side.

terms.def: London's Ultra Low Emission Zone — a daily charge on more polluting vehicles, the symbol of 'safety and sustainability' overreach for its opponents.
Freedom as the absence of interference — the kind this talk defends.

82.question: Did the left stop fighting exploitation and start competing over wounds — and is trauma culture capitalism's secret weapon?
82.why: Liu attacks her own side: the professional left's obsession with trauma, she argues, replaced class politics with a hierarchy of suffering that paralyses action and suits capital perfectly. From the origins of PTSD to Oprah, it's a genealogy of how wounds became credentials.
case: Trauma migrated from a clinical category for war and abuse to a universal idiom of identity; everyone has a wound and the wound confers authority.
Accommodating suffering became the left's programme, displacing the harder work of challenging power and building solidarity.
The professional-managerial class benefits: trauma expertise is a career, and it moralises class privilege as sensitivity.
Capitalism is untouched by any of it — which is why it funds the conferences.
objections: Trauma is real and its recognition was hard-won; mocking 'wound culture' can license the dismissal of actual victims.
Class politics did not vanish because of therapy; it lost because unions were broken and industries moved.
Liu's PMC critique can slide into a contempt for the educated that the right happily borrows.
The left she describes is mostly American and academic; the British trade-union left may not recognise itself.

speakers.name: Catherine Liu
speakers.stance: UC Irvine cultural theorist; Virtue Hoarders and Traumatized. Expect a Marxist critique of progressive culture delivered with relish. She also debates the manosphere (1:15pm) and institutions (4pm).

questions: What is the line between recognising trauma and weaponising it — who is on the right side of it?
If class politics is the answer, what does it say to people whose wounds are not economic?
Which institution of the left would you defund first?

reading.title: Virtue Hoarders
reading.note: The PMC critique the talk extends.

reading.title: The Empire of Trauma
reading.note: The scholarly history of how trauma became a moral category.

terms.def: Educated professionals — the Ehrenreichs' 1977 term — whom Liu accuses of moralising their own status.
The treatment of psychological wounds as the primary source of identity and moral authority.

83.question: Is physics a universal language any intelligent species would discover — or a description shaped by the particular minds that made it?
83.why: 'Mathematics is the language of the universe' is a cliché with a history. Whiteson's two-part course asks whether alien minds with different senses, bodies and histories would arrive at our physics — and what it means for the claim that physics describes reality rather than us.
case: Part 1: the idea that physics is universal was built by Galileo, Newton and Einstein; each step made choices (what counts as fundamental, what as noise) that another species might not.
Our physics is organised around what humans can perceive and build: distances, forces, particles; a species living in a fluid or at another scale might carve nature differently.
Part 2: if the carving is contingent, the 'unreasonable effectiveness' of maths is partly a selection effect — we keep the maths that works for us.
Yet some structure must be shared, or communication would be impossible; the question is how much.
objections: Convergence arguments: any species that builds rockets has to get the same equations right; the universe checks the answers.
'Shaped by our minds' can collapse into relativism about physics, which no working physicist believes.
Speculation about alien physics is unfalsifiable by design; it may illuminate philosophy of science more than physics.
The course is built on a popular book; expect breadth over rigour.

speakers.name: Daniel Whiteson
speakers.stance: UC Irvine particle physicist; co-author of Do Aliens Speak Physics? Expect an accessible, cartoon-assisted two-part course, honest about what is speculation. He appears three more times over the weekend.

questions: What is one part of physics you are confident an alien species would share, and one you are not?
Does the contingency of our concepts make physics less true, or only less final?
If an alien handed us their physics, how would we know it was correct?

reading.title: Do Aliens Speak Physics?
reading.note: The book behind the course.

reading.title: 'The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Mathematics in the Natural Sciences'
reading.note: The essay every discussion of this starts from.

terms.def: The claim that the laws we find would be found by any sufficiently capable observer.
Plato's image for concepts that match real structure — the question is whether ours do.

86.question: If we are always performing a self — on stage, on the feed — is there a true self underneath?
86.why: Stephens found fame at nineteen with Rizzle Kicks and has written about the cost of performing himself. Wilson has done the same from the other side of the wellness industry. The question they raise is now everyone's: the curated profile has made us all minor celebrities of our own lives.
case: Fame is the extreme case of a universal condition: a public self that others own, and a private self that has to be defended or disappears.
The performance is not fake — it is a real part of you — but treating it as the whole leads to the crash both speakers describe.
Social media hands everyone the machinery of fame without the money or the team; the pathologies scale.
There may be no fixed true self, only the practice of honesty about the roles — which is different from having none.
objections: Goffman showed in 1956 that all social life is performance; nothing about fame or feeds changes the philosophy.
Celebrities' accounts of the cost of fame are also performances, and lucrative ones.
The 'true self' is a Romantic idea; Buddhist and Humean views say the search is the problem.
The talk's two speakers agree with each other; the objections will have to come from the floor.

speakers.name: Jordan Stephens
speakers.stance: Musician (Rizzle Kicks), author of Avoidance, Drugs, Heartbreak and Dogs, mental-health advocate. Expect candour about fame, masculinity and performance.

speakers.name: Sarah Wilson
speakers.stance: Author (First, We Make the Beast Beautiful; This One Wild and Precious Life), former magazine editor and I Quit Sugar founder turned critic of wellness. Expect the social-philosophy frame.

questions: What was the moment you noticed the performed self had replaced the other one?
Is a teenager with 2,000 followers famous in the sense that matters?
If there is no true self, what are you being honest about?

reading.title: The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life
reading.note: Life as performance, before the internet.

reading.title: Avoidance, Drugs, Heartbreak and Dogs
reading.note: Stephens's memoir.

terms.def: Goffman's distinction between the performed public self and the region where the performance is prepared.
A one-sided relationship with a public figure — the audience's side of fame.

87.question: Can economics be rebuilt around the common good — where how we achieve goals matters as much as what they are?
87.why: Mazzucato made her name arguing the state is an entrepreneur, not a fixer of market failures. This talk goes further: an economy organised around collective goals, participation and reciprocity, with the process itself as part of the value. It is the intellectual programme behind 'mission economics'.
case: Value is created collectively — public research, infrastructure, education — and captured privately; the common good reverses the accounting.
Markets are outcomes of rules, not natural facts; shaping them towards shared goals (climate, health) is legitimate and effective.
How matters: goals reached by participation and reciprocity are more durable than goals imposed.
The evidence is in the mission-oriented programmes — from the moon landing to vaccine development — that public purpose can direct innovation.
objections: 'Common good' has no agreed content; who defines it, and what happens to those who disagree?
Mission-oriented policy has expensive failures (Concorde, industrial champions) that the success stories omit.
The state that Mazzucato trusts to set missions is the same one that struggles to build a railway.
Private investment follows returns; a common-good economy has to explain where the capital comes from.

speakers.name: Mariana Mazzucato
speakers.stance: UCL economist; The Entrepreneurial State, Mission Economy, The Big Con, The Common Good Economy. Advises the G20, WHO and UN. Expect a confident, policy-ready case with international examples. She debates inheritance at 2:30pm.

questions: Give an example of a mission that failed and what you learned from it.
Who decides the common good in a country split 50/50 on what it is?
What is the role of profit in your economy — tolerated, harnessed, or replaced?

reading.title: Mission Economy
reading.note: The programme in full.

reading.title: The Big Con
reading.note: Her attack on the consultancy industry — the 'how' argument in practice.

terms.def: Directing public and private investment at defined societal goals rather than fixing market failures case by case.
Value created collectively by public institutions — which Mazzucato argues economics systematically undercounts.

90.question: Can Wikipedia's bet — that people given trust and good faith will collectively pursue truth — survive misinformation and AI?
90.why: Wales built the largest encyclopaedia on a philosophy: neutrality, verifiability, and faith in strangers. Twenty-five years on, AI systems trained on Wikipedia produce confident falsehoods with no way to check them, and the site's model is under strain. Interviewed by Laura Kennedy.
case: Wikipedia works because of process, not authority: every claim needs a source, every edit can be reverted, and disputes are argued in the open.
Trust in strangers, bounded by rules, produced something no institution could; that is a finding about people, not just about software.
AI models that summarise without sources reverse the model: fluent, unverifiable, and often wrong.
The future of truth depends on institutions that show their working — and on people willing to do unpaid work for it.
objections: Wikipedia's neutrality is a policy enforced by a small, unrepresentative editor base; its blind spots (gender, the Global South) are documented.
The site's 'consensus' can be captured on contested topics; edit wars are power struggles, not truth-seeking.
AI companies took the corpus for free and now threaten the traffic that recruits editors — a problem Wales's philosophy did not anticipate.
Wales's faith in 'good faith' has a libertarian tilt that critics say underrates coordinated manipulation.

speakers.name: Jimmy Wales
speakers.stance: Co-founder of Wikipedia; The Seven Rules of Trust (2025). Expect optimism about people and worry about AI, and a defence of verifiability as the foundation of knowledge. He debates perspectivism at 4pm.

speakers.name: Laura Kennedy
speakers.stance: Interviews. Philosopher and writer (Some of Our Parts).

questions: What is the most important thing Wikipedia got wrong, and how was it fixed?
Should AI companies pay for the corpus they trained on — and would that save the editor base?
Is 'neutral point of view' a truth or a treaty?

reading.title: The Seven Rules of Trust
reading.note: His own account of what made Wikipedia work.

reading.title: 'Neutral point of view' (policy page)
reading.note: Read the policy the whole project rests on — it is shorter than you think.

terms.def: Wikipedia's rule that claims must be attributable to reliable published sources — 'verifiability, not truth'.
Representing significant views fairly and without editorial bias — the founding policy.

95.question: Is modernity a Western invention the rest of the world is catching up with — or does China have its own thousand-year tradition of thinking about knowledge, power and the good society?
95.why: Wang Hui is the intellectual most associated with China's 'New Left' and with the critique of the idea that history ends in Western liberalism. His claim that China's modernity is its own — not borrowed — is at once a scholarly thesis and a political one.
case: Chinese thought from the Song dynasty onward developed its own concepts of statecraft, knowledge and the public that do not map onto Western categories of 'tradition' and 'modernity'.
The 'catching up' story is Eurocentric history: it treats one path as the path.
China's twentieth-century revolutions were modern in their own terms — mass politics, equality, national unity — not imitations.
Understanding this matters now: a West that thinks China must converge will keep being surprised.
objections: The New Left's defence of China's 'own path' has been used to justify the Party's rejection of liberal reform; critics ask where the space for dissent is in the theory.
Modernity's key institutions — the nation state, industrial capitalism, science — did in fact spread from Europe; distinctiveness is not independence.
Wang's history is selective, as all intellectual histories are; the Confucian tradition also has liberal readings.
The talk may leave the audience with a thesis about history and no way to test it.

speakers.name: Wang Hui
speakers.stance: Tsinghua intellectual historian; China's New Order, The End of the Revolution, China from Empire to Nation-State. Expect a dense argument from the history of ideas. He also debates democracy (1:15pm) and progress (5:30pm).

questions: What in China's own tradition constrains power — and does the current state honour it?
If modernity is plural, is liberal democracy one modernity among others, or a mistake?
What would count as evidence that China had 'borrowed' rather than developed its modernity?

reading.title: China from Empire to Nation-State
reading.note: The introduction to his four-volume history, in English.

reading.title: The End of History and the Last Man
reading.note: The thesis Wang has spent a career opposing.

terms.def: Intellectuals critical of market reform's inequalities and of Western liberalism, associated with Wang Hui since the 1990s.
The view that modernisation has taken different institutional and cultural forms rather than one Western path.

96.question: Will the next revolution in physics come from rethinking the foundations — a hologram on the night sky, a mirror universe — rather than adding complexity?
96.why: General relativity and quantum mechanics have coexisted uneasily for a century. Pasterski and Turok each propose a foundational rethink: she describes four-dimensional physics as a hologram on the celestial sphere; he replaces the Big Bang singularity with a mirror between two universes. Two of the boldest current ideas, side by side.
case: Pasterski: celestial holography encodes scattering in our universe as a two-dimensional theory on the sky, offering a route to quantum gravity for realistic (flat) spacetime rather than the idealised anti-de Sitter case.

Turok: a CPT-symmetric universe — our universe and a mirror twin running backwards in time from the Big Bang — explains dark matter (right-handed neutrinos) and the matter–antimatter asymmetry without inflation.
Both reject the 'add a field, add a dimension' habit of recent decades in favour of symmetry and simplicity.
Both make claims that could be tested: Turok's predictions for neutrino masses, Pasterski's structural constraints on scattering.
objections: Celestial holography is a research programme, not yet a theory; critics note it has not produced a new prediction about the world.
Turok's mirror universe is elegant but young; the mainstream still regards inflation as better supported by the CMB.
'Radical rethinking' is what every generation of theorists says; the test is decades of data.
Two speakers, one hour, no host: expect two mini-lectures rather than an exchange.

speakers.name: Sabrina Pasterski
speakers.stance: Perimeter Institute theoretical physicist, leader of the celestial holography programme, widely billed as 'the next Einstein'. Expect precision and ambition; she gives her own talk at 3pm on automating theory with AI.

speakers.name: Neil Turok
speakers.stance: Higgs Chair at Edinburgh; The Universe Within; the mirror-universe model with Latham Boyle. Expect a lucid case against inflation and for simplicity. His solo talk is at 3:30pm.

questions: What observation, feasible in the next decade, would confirm or kill your idea?
Do your two proposals conflict, or could both be true?
What did the last century of 'adding complexity' get right?

reading.title: The Universe Within
reading.note: His Massey Lectures — the sensibility behind the mirror universe.

reading.title: 'Celestial Holography' (review article)
reading.note: Technical, but the introduction is readable.

terms.def: The idea that a region's physics can be described by a theory on its boundary; celestial holography applies it to the sky at infinity.
The combined symmetry of charge, parity and time reversal that any relativistic quantum theory must respect — the basis of Turok's mirror universe.

98.question: Can economics ever be a mathematical science like physics — or is economic life irreducibly human, made of language, ethics and persuasion?
98.why: McCloskey spent a career inside mainstream economics before turning on its pretensions to physics-like precision. This two-part course traces how the discipline came to model itself on mechanics and argues that markets run on talk — 'sweet talk' — as much as on prices.
case: Part 1: economics adopted physics envy in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries — equilibrium, optimisation, statistical significance — and gained rigour at the cost of realism.
A quarter of economic activity is persuasion: managers, lawyers, salespeople, teachers talk people into things; the models leave it out.
Part 2: the Great Enrichment came from ideas and rhetoric — the dignity of the bourgeois — not from capital accumulation, which is what the equations count.
An economics that took ethics and language seriously would predict less and explain more.
objections: Formal models have real successes — auctions, matching markets, monetary policy; 'humanities economics' offers no substitute for them.
McCloskey's ideas-first history of growth is contested by economic historians who point to coal, colonies and capital.
Rhetoric-centred economics can slide into stories chosen for their charm; that is the vice she diagnoses in her opponents.
Her liberalism (Cato Institute) shapes which human factors she counts — persuasion, not power.

speakers.name: Deirdre McCloskey
speakers.stance: Economist and historian; The Bourgeois Virtues, Bourgeois Dignity, Bourgeois Equality, Why Liberalism Works; Isaiah Berlin Chair at Cato. Expect wit, erudition and a liberal's confidence. She debates progress at 5:30pm.

questions: Which mainstream model would you keep, and why does it survive your critique?
If rhetoric drove the Great Enrichment, why did it happen in Britain and Holland first?
How would a humanities economics have handled the 2008 crisis differently?

reading.title: The Rhetoric of Economics
reading.note: Where the critique began.

reading.title: Bourgeois Equality
reading.note: The ideas-first account of modern growth.

terms.def: The aspiration of social sciences to the mathematical form and predictive power of physics.
McCloskey's term for the thirtyfold rise in living standards since 1800.

100.question: Every complex civilisation before ours has collapsed — is ours next, and what does honest preparation look like?
100.why: Wilson's argument is not that collapse is coming next year but that refusing to consider it is itself the danger. Drawing on 200 conversations with philosophers, game theorists and spiritual leaders, she offers a framework for living well inside systemic breakdown.
case: The historical record — Rome, the Maya, the Bronze Age — shows complex societies fail from converging stresses, and ours faces climate, debt, and institutional decay at once.
Denial is the dominant response and the worst one; clarity about risk is the precondition for purpose.
Collapse is a process, not an event; the question is how to act with integrity through it, not how to escape.
Meaning under breakdown comes from community, honesty and reduced dependence — a minimalist ethic with old roots.
objections: Collapse literature has a poor forecasting record; past civilisations' failures were regional, and ours is the first with global science.
'Every civilisation collapsed' is a survivorship framing — most also transformed, merged or slowly changed.
Framing the future as breakdown can be its own form of denial: of agency, of the boring work of adaptation.
The self-help register ('clarity, purpose') sits uneasily with the scale of the claim.

speakers.name: Sarah Wilson
speakers.stance: Author and 'social philosopher' (This One Wild and Precious Life; First, We Make the Beast Beautiful), host of the Wild podcast. Expect an accessible synthesis of collapse scholarship with a personal ethic. She also appears at 10:30am on fame.

questions: What is the single indicator you'd watch to tell 'decline' from 'collapse'?
Which past civilisation did collapse well, and what did its people do right?
What should someone in this tent do differently on Monday?

reading.title: The Collapse of Complex Societies
reading.note: The scholarly foundation of the collapse argument — complexity's diminishing returns.

reading.title: This One Wild and Precious Life
reading.note: Her framework for living with the crises.

terms.def: Multiple systemic crises interacting so that the whole is worse than the sum — the current term of art.
A rapid, significant loss of an established level of sociopolitical complexity.

109.question: How does power work when AI can set the agenda and shape what people want — and is Lukes's three-dimensional theory still enough?
109.why: Power: A Radical View (1974) distinguished visible conflict, agenda control, and the shaping of desires. AI systems now do the third at scale, without a human intending it. Lukes revisits his theory with philosopher Audrey Borowski for the new edition.
case: The third dimension — securing compliance by shaping beliefs and wants — was always the most important and the least visible; recommender systems industrialise it.
AI power is exercised without an agent: nobody decides what you want, yet your wants are shaped — a challenge to the theory's focus on human intention.
Agenda-setting (the second dimension) is now automated: what appears in feeds and search decides what gets discussed.
The remedy is the same as ever — making the invisible visible — but the tools have to be new.
objections: Persuasion, advertising and propaganda have shaped wants for a century; AI changes scale, not kind.
A theory in which power operates without anyone exercising it risks becoming unfalsifiable — everything is 'power'.
People push back: algorithmic influence is measurable and smaller than the panic suggests.
Lukes's framework was built for politics and workplaces; whether it fits machine learning is exactly what needs argument.

speakers.name: Steven Lukes
speakers.stance: Political and social theorist (NYU); Power: A Radical View, now in a new edition. Expect conceptual precision and reluctance to overclaim.

speakers.name: Audrey Borowski
speakers.stance: Cambridge philosopher and historian of Leibniz and computation (Leibniz in His World). Expect the long view on machines that reason and the humans who defer to them. She also debates AI hype on Saturday.

questions: Who holds power when a recommender system shapes an election — the company, the engineer, the model, no one?
What would count as evidence that AI has changed what people want, rather than only what they see?
Does your theory need a fourth dimension, or a different first one?

reading.title: Power: A Radical View
reading.note: Short and foundational.

reading.title: The Age of Surveillance Capitalism
reading.note: The case that behaviour-shaping is the business model.

terms.def: Lukes: winning visible conflicts; keeping issues off the agenda; shaping what people believe and want.
Software that ranks content for each user — the third dimension of power, automated.

115.question: Is the serious novel in terminal decline — and if readers disappear, do we lose the capacity for depth of thought with them?
115.why: Fewer than half of American adults read a book a year; the difficult novel has been pushed to the margins by media that never asks anyone to sit with difficulty. Self, whose novels demand exactly that, calls it a civilisational crisis; Kavenna asks whether anything can be done.
case: The novel trained a form of attention — solitary, sustained, ambiguous — that nothing else does; losing the readers loses the faculty.
Digital media's 'synthetic fluff' is not competition but replacement: same hours, opposite effect on the mind.
The market has followed: publishers reward the personal, the short and the algorithm-friendly.
This is not nostalgia: societies without deep readers make worse decisions and shallower art.
objections: The serious novel was always a minority pursuit; the mass readership of the past was for melodrama and romance.
Reading has moved, not died — long-form audio, fan fiction, serialised online writing are huge and not all fluff.
'Depth of thought' is not the novel's monopoly; philosophy, film and argument train it too.
Novelists announcing the death of the novel is a genre with a long history and no fatalities.

speakers.name: Will Self
speakers.stance: Novelist (Umbrella, Shark, Phone; Elaine) and essayist; has argued since 2014 that the literary novel is dying. Expect erudition, pessimism and pleasure in both.

speakers.name: Joanna Kavenna
speakers.stance: Novelist and essayist (Zed, A Field Guide to Reality). Expect the questioner's role, with her own scepticism about tech.

questions: What is the last novel that a large public argued about — and what replaced that argument?
If the novel dies, what inherits its work?
Is your pessimism about readers or about writers?

reading.title: 'The novel is dead (this time it's for real)'
reading.note: The essay this talk descends from.

reading.title: Zed
reading.note: A novel about the algorithms doing the replacing.

terms.def: Sustained, reflective reading that builds inference and empathy — Maryanne Wolf's term.
Fiction valued for form and difficulty rather than genre pleasures — the thing said to be dying.

116.question: Can theoretical physics be automated — and what is celestial holography, the programme Pasterski is trying to automate?
116.why: The 'next Einstein' is not working alone: she is building AI and robotic tools to do parts of theoretical physics. The talk is two things at once — an introduction to celestial holography and a report from the frontier of machine-assisted theory.
case: Celestial holography reformulates scattering in flat spacetime as a two-dimensional conformal theory on the celestial sphere; symmetries do the heavy lifting.
Much of theoretical work — checking identities, exploring parameter spaces, proposing conjectures — is mechanisable; AI can search where humans cannot.
Automation changes what a theorist is: a designer of questions and constraints rather than a calculator.
The stakes: quantum gravity in our actual universe, not a toy one.
objections: AI systems have so far produced no new physical theory; they optimise within frameworks humans built.
Celestial holography's payoff is still conjectural; automation of a programme is not evidence for it.
The 'next Einstein' billing is a media label; Einstein's advances were conceptual, which is what automation is worst at.
Robotics in theoretical physics may be a metaphor; ask what the robot actually does.

speakers.name: Sabrina Pasterski
speakers.stance: Perimeter Institute physicist leading the celestial holography programme; MIT and Harvard trained; has spoken about using AI in theory. Expect a technical talk made accessible, and confidence about automation. She also appears at 12:30 with Turok and in Saturday's AI debate.

questions: What is the first result you'd credit to the automated system rather than a human?
Which part of theory-building do you think can never be automated?
What would celestial holography predict that could be observed?

reading.title: 'Celestial Holography' (review article)
reading.note: The programme in the authors' words.

reading.title: The Road to Reality
reading.note: The mathematical background, if you want it, from the man debating inflation at 10:30.

terms.def: The two-dimensional sky at infinity on which celestial holography encodes four-dimensional scattering.
Symmetries of spacetime at large distances (BMS symmetries) that structure the holographic dictionary.

121.question: What if the Big Bang is not a beginning but a mirror — with a twin universe running backwards in time on the other side?
121.why: Turok and Boyle's CPT-symmetric universe proposes that the Big Bang is a moment of reflection, not a singularity: a universe of antimatter runs backwards in time on the other side. One idea, they claim, explains dark matter, the matter–antimatter asymmetry, and does away with inflation.
case: The laws of physics are CPT-symmetric; a universe that respects that symmetry through the Big Bang is the simplest cosmology consistent with them.
Dark matter falls out as a right-handed neutrino with a predicted mass — a testable claim.
Why matter exists at all: the asymmetry is shared with the mirror universe, so the total is balanced.
No inflaton, no multiverse, no fine-tuned initial state — the problems inflation was invented to solve dissolve.
objections: The model is new and has a small research community; inflation has forty years of development and fits the CMB well.
'Running backwards in time' is a symmetry statement, not a second universe anyone can visit; critics ask what is physically claimed.
The neutrino-mass prediction could fail, and the model's fate depends on it.
Elegance is not evidence — the point Hossenfelder makes about all of theoretical physics.

speakers.name: Neil Turok
speakers.stance: Higgs Chair of Theoretical Physics, Edinburgh; former director of the Perimeter Institute; The Universe Within. Expect the full case against inflation and for simplicity, delivered with unusual clarity. He debates Penrose on inflation at 10:30 and joins Pasterski at 12:30.

questions: What is the neutrino mass your model predicts, and when will experiment tell us?
In what sense does the mirror universe exist — could anything from it affect us?
If Penrose and you both reject inflation, where do you disagree?

reading.title: 'CPT-Symmetric Universe'
reading.by: Latham Boyle, Kieran Finn and Neil Turok, Physical Review Letters (2018)
reading.note: The paper; the abstract is readable.

reading.title: Cycles of Time
reading.note: The other anti-inflation cosmology on the bill.

terms.def: A point of infinite density where general relativity breaks down — what the mirror universe replaces.
A hypothetical heavy neutrino partner; in Turok's model, the dark matter.

124.question: Is the need to matter — the source of art, ambition and violence alike — a biological drive we must learn to satisfy without turning on each other?
124.why: Goldstein has argued for decades that 'mattering' is the hidden variable in human life: why people make art no one sees and why they kill to be noticed. In conversation with David Edmonds, she connects the philosophy of meaning to the politics of resentment.
case: The need to matter is not vanity but a condition of agency: to act is to assume one's acts count.
Cultures supply 'mattering maps' — routes to significance through achievement, belonging, virtue; when the maps fail, people take violent shortcuts.
Philosophy's old question 'what is a meaningful life?' is the practical question 'how do I matter, and to whom?'
The task is to widen the routes — recognition, work, community — rather than to shame the need.
objections: 'Mattering' may relabel status-seeking; evolutionary psychology already explains it, less flatteringly.
Some ethical traditions (Stoic, Buddhist) counsel releasing the need to matter, not feeding it.
The link from thwarted significance to violence is plausible but selective; most people who don't matter don't kill.
The concept is broad enough to explain everything — a warning sign.

speakers.name: Rebecca Goldstein
speakers.stance: Philosopher and novelist (Plato at the Googleplex; The Mattering Instinct is her long-running theme), MacArthur Fellow. Expect the argument made through stories and Spinoza. She also debates the self in literature on Saturday.

speakers.name: David Edmonds
speakers.stance: Interviews. Philosopher and broadcaster (Wittgenstein's Poker; Parfit).

questions: How do you tell a healthy need to matter from a dangerous one — before the violence?
What does a society do for people whose mattering map has failed?
Is the philosopher's need to matter different in kind from anyone else's?

reading.title: Plato at the Googleplex
reading.note: Where 'mattering' gets its fullest treatment.

reading.title: Parfit: A Philosopher and His Mission to Save Morality
reading.note: The interviewer's own book on a man consumed by mattering to the future.

terms.def: Goldstein's term for the drive to be significant — to have one's existence and actions count.
A culture's shared sense of what makes a life significant, and who gets to be.

125.question: 'Study hard, master your field, build expertise' — is that advice now dangerously out of date, and what should education be for in a world of intelligent machines?
125.why: Susskind argues we are preparing children for a world that no longer exists: expertise that machines will reproduce, careers that will not last. His vision rebuilds education from scratch for humans who share the world with AI.
case: The traditional route — deep expertise in one field — is precisely what AI automates first; the machines are best at what the graduate is trained to do.
Education should aim at what remains: judgement, adaptation, the ability to work with machines and to ask what is worth doing.
Career as a ladder is over; education for a portfolio of roles across a long life is the replacement.
This is an opportunity: a curriculum built around meaning and purpose, not credentials.
objections: Predictions of the end of expertise have been wrong repeatedly; AI still needs experts to check it.
'Judgement and adaptability' are taught by mastering something first; you cannot skip to wisdom.
Education reforms are slow and political; 'rebuilt from scratch' is a phrase, not a plan.
The Gove position (Saturday) — knowledge first — is the direct opposite, and has more evidence on attainment.

speakers.name: Daniel Susskind
speakers.stance: Oxford economist (A World Without Work; Growth: A Reckoning; The Future of the Professions with Richard Susskind). Expect a clear, forward-looking argument. He also debates the educated elite on Saturday.

questions: What should a fourteen-year-old be doing on Monday that they are not doing now?
Which existing skill will hold its value longest, and why?
If expertise is automated, who checks the machine?

reading.title: A World Without Work
reading.note: The automation argument.

reading.title: The Future of the Professions
reading.note: Why expert work is the first to change.

terms.def: AI replacing tasks within jobs rather than whole occupations — the mechanism Susskind analyses.
Using qualifications as proxies for ability — the thing a rebuilt education would drop.

128.question: Are nations finished as the focus of power — and if American hegemony, Western debt and tech firms have shattered the system, what replaces it?
128.why: Dasgupta's After Nations argues that the nation-state system that seemed eternal is breaking under forces it cannot contain: capital that moves faster than states, tech firms acting as geopolitical actors, and the return of Chinese power. He looks back to the fall of empires for what comes next.
case: The nation state is a recent form (two centuries) that was universalised after 1945 and is now failing at its core jobs: controlling money, information and violence.
Western debt and American decline remove the guarantor of the system; nothing replaces it.
Tech firms and platforms are political actors — they run infrastructure, communications and now warfare — without being nations.
History's precedents — the end of empires — show transitions are long, violent and produce forms nobody predicted.
objections: Nations are also resurgent: borders, tariffs, nationalism and war show the state's monopoly on force is alive.
'After nations' has been announced by globalisers for thirty years; the state kept coming back.
The alternative is left vague; a 'new conception of power' is a promissory note.
Novelists writing political theory can mistake narrative force for argument.

speakers.name: Rana Dasgupta
speakers.stance: Novelist and essayist (Solo; Capital: The Eruption of Delhi; After Nations). Expect a sweeping, literary argument from history. He also joins the climate 'doom loop' conversation at 5:30pm.

questions: Name the power that has replaced the state in one specific domain — and who holds it accountable?
Are borders and tariffs the death rattle of nations or their revival?
What did the end of the Roman or Ottoman order look like to someone living through it?

reading.title: After Nations
reading.note: The book the talk is drawn from.

reading.title: The Nation-State and Violence
reading.note: The classic account of what the nation state is and does.

135.question: Can democracies break the climate doom loop — where disasters fuel the discontent that empowers the politicians who slow the response?
135.why: The expectation was that floods and fires would force action. Instead they feed anger, anger feeds populists, populists slow the transition, and the disasters worsen. A live recording of the Overshoot podcast with Laybourn as host and Dasgupta as guest.
case: Climate impacts are political before they are physical: they raise prices, displace people and erode trust, which anti-climate movements harvest.
The transition itself creates losers who vote; ignoring that is how the loop tightens.
Breaking the loop means building resilience and fairness into the transition — protection for the exposed, not just targets.
Dasgupta's frame: this is happening as the nation-state order itself weakens, so the actors who could respond are losing capacity.
objections: The loop is asserted from a few cases; elsewhere disasters have strengthened climate politics (Australia after the fires, in part).
Populist backlash is driven by energy prices and immigration more than by climate disasters as such.
'Resilience and fairness' is what every party says; the difficulty is paying for it.
A podcast recording rewards conversation over confrontation; look for the moment of disagreement.
